query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin (~2–5 µm) oxide-based surface coating (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) via pulsed laser or sputter deposition on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will establish a stable tribofilm, thereby enabling a consistently low coefficient of friction and low wear rate from room temperature through 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, uncoated polycrystalline CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in as-processed state.
generation.intervention: Apply a 2–5 µm nanolaminated oxide layer by pulsed laser or magnetron sputtering, ensuring strong adhesion to the CoCrFeNi substrate.
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk or reciprocating sliding tests in air, spanning 25–800 °C and moderate normal loads (e.g., 10–30 N).
generation.structural_mediator: An adherent oxide surface layer that can form or regenerate under frictional heating and protect the ductile HEA substrate.
generation.mechanism: Below ~600 °C, the protective oxide coating shields the alloy from adhesive wear, while at elevated temperatures (≥600 °C) the coating develops a stable tribo-oxide interface that mitigates oxidation fatigue and reduces friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated material will exhibit significantly lower friction (remaining relatively stable over the entire temperature range) and reduced wear rates, thus overcoming the conventional rise in oxidation-driven wear at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Uncoated CoCrFeNi HEA tested under the same tribological conditions, exhibiting rising friction and wear above ~600 °C.
generation.boundary: Viability demonstrated for sliding contact in air up to ~800 °C; coating integrity may be uncertain beyond this temperature or in highly corrosive environments.
generation.uncertainty: If coating spallation occurs under very high loads or thermal cycles beyond 800 °C, the protective effect might be lost, leading to wear rates similar to the uncoated alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled pin-on-disk wear test on coated and uncoated CoCrFeNi samples from 25 °C to 800 °C at 100 °C increments, monitoring friction coefficient in real-time and measuring wear volume post-test.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at each temperature setpoint
Post-test mass loss or volume loss of sample and counterpart
Microstructural analysis of coatings and interfaces (SEM/EDS) to evaluate coating stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If friction coefficients and wear rates of the coated samples approach those of the uncoated reference across the 25–800 °C range, then the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.

decision.trend: Researchers tackling high-temperature sliding wear in CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys have explored adding reactive elements to form hard intermetallic phases (as in W-doped AlCoCrFeNi). While such alloy modifications can enhance high-temperature hardness and wear resistance, friction remains difficult to control across the entire 20–800 °C range. In particular, adding W improved wear resistance at elevated temperatures yet introduced friction fluctuations, leaving open the challenge of achieving both low wear and low, stable friction in CoCrFeNi-like matrices from room temperature to 800 °C.
decision.unsolved: A reliable method to maintain simultaneously low friction and low wear in CoCrFeNi-based alloys through the large 20–800 °C range remains elusive. Approaches targeting the bulk composition can raise mechanical strength or hamper wear, but often fail to ensure stable lubrication and friction control across all temperatures.
decision.lever: Deposit a ~2–5 μm multifunctional oxide-based coating (e.g., a nanolaminated Al2O3 or Cr2O3 top layer) on the CoCrFeNi matrix by pulsed laser deposition or magnetron sputtering, engineered to form a stable, self-lubricating tribofilm at ≥600 °C. Ensure careful control of coating thickness and substrate-interface adhesion for robust high-temperature performance.
decision.why: Building on evidence that stable oxide interphases enhance high-temperature wear resistance and friction control (as seen in AlCoCrFeNi under 800 °C conditions), a well-bonded oxide-based surface layer can suppress oxidation and reduce tribo-oxidation fluctuations. This aligns with the question’s need to maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C without changing the alloy’s bulk composition.
